newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan suburb like ghost town after child's murder.
newsitem.headline: Japan suburb like ghost town after child's murder.

text.p: A suburb of Kobe in western Japan was like a ghost town on Sunday with the killer of a decapitated 11-year-old boy on the loose, residents said.
Jun Hase left his home in residential district of Suma shortly after noon on May 24, saying he was going to see his grandfather.
Three days later his mutilated head was found at the foot of an iron gate of a nearby junior high school.
A note was written on at least two pieces of paper folded and placed inside the boy's mouth.
The body was later found at a television antenna compound near his elementary school.
Residents said the Suma area was very quiet on Sunday, with few children venturing outside their homes.
"This place looks like a ghost town," said one 33-year-old mother. "Both us parents and children are in fear."
Residents had been handed portable alarms to give to their children.
The note, released by police on Saturday, spoke of the killer's enjoyment of killing and said that a "long-standing grudge" would be settled by the "flow of blood".
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has vowed an all-out police effort to catch the killer.

In March, two young schoolgirls were attacked by a knife-wielding man near the school where the head was found and one 10-year-old died. Police said there was no evidence so far that the cases were linked.

Some criminologists speculated that the suspect was a man in his 30s with a deep grudge against the education system because of the repeated mention of schools in the note and the fact that he left the head in front of a school.

"I think this man is in his late 20s or early 30s who does not have a stable job and is someone who has a deep grudge against the school that he went to," said Sophia University criminology professor Shoji Watanabe.
"For this type of killer, what appears to be absolutely abnormal to the commoner is just a mere method to attract wide public attention," said Ryuzo Saki, author of criminal non-fiction books.
"There is a grave possibility that this kind of criminal can escalate his actions and hit again," Saki told the daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun.
